claims.text: The proposed nanoparticles have an equiatomic PtAuPdAgCu composition.
The PtAuPdAgCu nanoparticles are synthesized by high-energy ball milling of the metal precursors and annealing at 800°C.
Annealing at 800°C provides sufficient atomic mobility for elemental diffusion in PtAuPdAgCu nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching after high-temperature treatment can preserve a homogeneous multielement alloy and suppress elemental segregation or phase separation.
Rapid ice-water quenching will kinetically freeze a homogeneous high-entropy solid solution in annealed PtAuPdAgCu nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching halts diffusion and phase separation in the nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching preserves a state of high configurational entropy.
A disordered, high-configurational-entropy state provides synergistic multimetal catalytic sites.
Slow furnace cooling allows thermodynamically driven elemental segregation and phase separation.
Elemental segregation or phase separation reduces catalytic performance.
Rapidly quenched PtAuPdAgCu nanoparticles will have a more homogeneous atomic distribution than slowly furnace-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have higher catalytic activity, such as increased turnover frequency, than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have improved catalytic stability relative to slowly cooled nanoparticles.
The proposed cooling-rate effect should hold around an annealing temperature of 800°C when quenching and furnace-cooling rates are sharply differentiated.
The proposed mechanism applies to equiatomic noble-metal HEA nanoparticles within time-temperature regimes where segregation can be kinetically suppressed.
Nanoparticle size distribution and support interactions may influence formation or catalytic performance independently of cooling rate.
